criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) service delivery and governance in the context of disaster risk reduction in Karonga Town, Malawi.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain/literal wording of Criterion 2 ('legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor') because it examines institutional mandates under the Local Government Act and Water Works Act, dissolution of Karonga Town Council in 2009, incomplete decentralization, municipal financing, and the absence of a national WASH law and town by-laws. However, it fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading because it analyzes broad municipal/sector WASH-for-disaster-risk-reduction governance (budget constraints, stakeholder coordination/council bypass, M&E capacity, advocacy, NIMBY/EIA barriers to waste disposal sites, and unregulated yard burials) rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden on users, tenure/documentation rules, tariffs, discretion, or access enforcement).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains original empirical data collected from October 2015 to March 2016 via semi-structured questionnaires with 35 purposively selected WASH stakeholders, two consultative workshops (30 local and 50 national stakeholders), and documentary analysis.
criterion_notes.c4: Does not report an empirical outcome measuring household or community water or sanitation access, connection, service availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion linked to a governance factor. Primary empirical outcomes are stakeholder governance roles (Fig. 4), priority rankings (Fig. 5), stakeholder collaboration challenges (Table 2), and perceived institutional bottlenecks to WASH governance (Fig. 6); household coverage figures in Section 3.1 are secondary background statistics cited from prior reports (with safe-water coverage drop from 65% to 51% attributed to 2009 earthquake and flood damage) alongside hospital disease counts (Table 1).
criterion_notes.c5: Study design (mixed-methods stakeholder survey, workshops, and document review), setting, institutional stakeholder sample (n = 35), macro-governance exposures, and stakeholder-perception outcomes are clearly identifiable, though household/community access outcomes are not measured.

evidence_quotes.quote: This paper presents a critical analysis of the water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) governance and service delivery situation in the context of disaster risk reduction in Karonga Town in Malawi.

Despite the availability of a number of policies used to regulate WASH governance for disaster risk reduction in Malawi, there is no legislative framework for the town because of dissolution of the town council. At national level, there was no WASH legislation to directly support the water and sanitation policies and WASH governance in general.
Data was collected through stakeholder consultations and documentary analysis from October 2015 to March 2016.

Analysis of policy documents, policy briefs, internal administrative documents, technical reports, policy guides, plans, strategies, and laws was done to elicit additional information on WASH governance.
The earthquake and ﬂoods caused non-functionality of water points (both taps and boreholes) and caused many households to resort to unsafe water sources such as the lake, rivers and shallow wells.
Of the stakeholders who participated in the questionnaire survey, 85% (Fig. 6) stated that there is very high resistance by communities to have waste disposal sites close to their residences.

raw_response.exposure: Macro-level municipal WASH-for-disaster-risk-reduction governance challenges: dissolution of Karonga Town Council in 2009 and reliance on rural district/traditional structures, overlapping mandates between Karonga District Council and Northern Region Water Board, incomplete decentralization, inadequate council WASH budgets, NGO council-bypass, and absence of a national WASH law and municipal WASH by-laws
raw_response.outcome: Stakeholder-reported WASH governance roles (Fig. 4), priority rankings of governance interests (Fig. 5), interagency engagement challenges (Table 2), and perceived institutional/capacity barriers to WASH governance and service delivery for disaster risk reduction (Fig. 6), alongside secondary hospital WASH-related disease counts following the 2009 earthquake and floods (Table 1)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Karonga Town, Malawi; purposive sample of 35 key institutional WASH stakeholders (50% local government, 21% NGOs, 17% central government, 8% community leaders/local entrepreneurs/service providers, 4% public utility providers), plus consultative workshops in Karonga Town (30 stakeholders) and at the national level (50 stakeholders)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded primarily under E03 (Wrong exposure) under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification, and secondarily fails Criterion 4 (Wrong outcome). While the study passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 by examining municipal WASH governance, statutory mandates, town council dissolution, incomplete decentralization, and missing WASH legislation/bylaws in Karonga Town, Malawi, it investigates broad sector-level disaster risk reduction governance (council budget shortfalls, NGO coordination/council bypass, M&E capacity, advocacy, solid waste siting, and unregulated yard burials) rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access. Even under the plain reading of Criterion 2, the overall decision remains exclude because the primary empirical study (35 institutional stakeholders) measures stakeholder governance roles, priority rankings, and perceived governance bottlenecks rather than household or community water or sanitation access, connection, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion outcomes (coverage statistics in Section 3.1 are cited strictly from secondary reports, with the drop from 65% to 51% attributed to earthquake and flood damage).
raw_response.study_design: Mixed-methods empirical case study combining a semi-structured stakeholder questionnaire survey (n = 35), two stakeholder consultative workshops (n = 30 local; n = 50 national), and documentary/policy analysis
